newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Huge potential seen in Brazil drinks market.
newsitem.headline: Huge potential seen in Brazil drinks market.

text.p: Representatives of Brazil's beverage industry said low consumption levels of alcoholic and soft drinks showed the Brazilian market had huge potential to expand as standards of living improved.

In 1995, sales of soft drinks and beer jumped 25 and 42.1 percent, respectively, in volume terms as a direct result of Brazil's 1994 anti-inflation Real Plan which bestowed greater buying power on low income earners, they said.

"Brazil is a country of low per capita income which restricts drinks consumption. Brazilians drink water from the tap," said the executive director of Brazil's Soft Drinks Industry Association (ABIR), Carlos Alberto Cabral. "But low consumption levels mean the market has enormous potential."
In 1996, Brazilians consumed per capita 59 liters of soft drinks, 50 liters of beer, 1.7 liters of wine and 10 liters of spirits.
Brazil is Latin America's largest country has a population of approximately 160 million.

These figures compare with the highest annual per capita consumptions of 181 liters of soft drinks in the United States, 170 liters of beer in the Czech Republic and 70 liters of wine in Italy and France, ABIR said. In spirits, Brazil ranks 10th after Russia, the Scandinavian countries and others.
In the last three years, Brazil's soft drinks and beer industry have invested $1.3 billion and $3 billion, respectively, to increase and improve production, and further large investments are planned.
Soft drinks manufacturers plan to invest $5 billion by the year 2000, while seven new beer breweries are due to come online in the next year and a half worth $1 billion in investments.

Soft drink sales of 9.9 billion liters in 1996 worth $6.8 billion are expected to increase eight percent this year, while sales of spirits worth $2 billion are seen to grow five percent and wine sales of $450 million increase 14 percent to 292 million liters.

Sales of beer worth $8.8 billion are seen to remain stable in 1997 at eight billion liters, but are expected to rise to 10 billion liters by 2000, according to Marcos Mesquita, superintendent of Brazil's National Beer Syndicate.

He said the industry hoped to lower beer prices and increase sales by negotiating with Brazil's states to reduce the amount of tax paid on beer. Taxes account for 32 percent of the retail price of beer.
